attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you finish the tilemap design by adding a border with a new  tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What type of tile do you think would work well as the border for this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use both the paint and fill tools in the tilemap editor to complete the tilemap. 


💡In this tilemap, the border tiles will function as walls, without actually using the wall feature in MakeCode. Later in the activity, the ninja will use an [on sprite overlaps tile] instead of an [on sprite hits wall] container to code the Player sprite’s interaction with the border tiles.
steps.instructions:
Finish the tilemap design!


Edit the tilemap by clicking the square in the [set tilemap to] block. Select one new tile to use as the border around the blue checkerboard tiles already on the tilemap. Use only one tile type to make sure the code for the border works later on! 


Click ▶ to see the tilemap with the border around it appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the starting position of the Player and Coin sprites on different colored tiles?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Will the Player and Coin sprite ever appear on the same tile from the start? Why or why not?

❓ Why might it be helpful to place the Player and Coin sprites on different colored tiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Explain to the ninja that randomness can add an element of surprise to a game. By setting the Player and Coin sprites on different colored tiles, it prevents them from overlapping immediately when the game begins.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by setting the Player and Coin sprites’ positions on the tilemap!


Drag a [place sprite on top of random tile] block under each [set sprite to] block. Click the gray box to select one of the solid square tile colors for the Player sprite to start on, then select the other solid square tile color for the Coin sprite to start on.


Click ▶ to see the 2 sprites appear on different colored tiles on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type 16 for the on right button pressed and -16 for the on left button pressed parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How is using the [on button pressed] containers different than using the [move sprite with buttons] block?

❓What else might happen differently when the user presses each direction button?

❓What tool can be used to flip an image horizontally in the image editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to duplicate the entire code block by right clicking on the container (and selecting “duplicate”). Remind the ninja to change the direction selected in the dropdown menu, select the x property, update the parameter, and select the correct facing image in the [set sprite image to] block.

💡Point out to the ninja that there is not a right-facing Player sprite image in the Gallery. As a result, they should select the left-facing image and use the flip horizontal tool to create a right-facing image.
steps.instructions:
Use [on button pressed] event blocks to move the Player sprite right and left, 1 tile at a time across the tilemap.


Drag an [on button pressed] container out, then click the drop down menu to select [right] to control the right direction button. Drag a [change sprite [x]] block into the container, and update the sprite name in the (sprite) bubble. In the parameter, type the number 16—the width of one tile on the tilemap. Drag a [set sprite image to] block into the container and select an image of the Player sprite facing left from the Gallery. Once selected, use the flip horizontal tool to create a right-facing image.


Repeat these steps to code the [left] direction button. Use the number -16 as the x parameter to make the sprite move left.


Click ▶ then test out the right and left direction buttons!

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the “y” property in the [change sprite [x]] block, and update the parameters to reflect up and down movement?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How is setting the up/down direction buttons, different than setting the left/right direction buttons?

❓ Which directions include a negative value in the parameter? Why?

❓ Does the Player sprite’s movement work as expected?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to duplicate the entire code block by right clicking on the container (and selecting “duplicate”). Remind the ninja to change the direction selected in the dropdown menu, select the y property, update the parameter, and select the correct facing image in the [set sprite image to] block.

💡Prompt the Ninja to test out the project to ensure the Player sprite’s movement is working as expected. The Player sprite should be able to move left, right, up, and down, one tile at a time. The sprite’s image should update correctly, based on the direction moved.
steps.instructions:
Use additional event blocks to move the Player sprite up and down, 1 tile at a time across the tilemap.


Drag another [on button pressed] container out, then select [down] from the drop down menu. Drag a [change sprite [x]] block into the container, then select y from the drop down menu to move the sprite up and down along the y axis. In the parameter, type the number 16 to make the sprite move down one entire tile on the tilemap. Drag a [set sprite image to] block into the container and select an image of the Player sprite facing down, or forward, from the Gallery.


Repeat these steps to code the [up] direction button. Use the number -16 as the y parameter to make the sprite move up.


Click ▶ then test out the up and down direction buttons!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the border tile you used in Step 1 to program something to happen when the Player sprite overlaps with the wall?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you test out different parameters in the [camera shake] block?

❓ Did you duplicate the [place sprite on random tile] from the [on start] container?

❓ Did you drag the (sprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Ask the ninja to consider what would happen if they did not drag the (sprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block and why this approach is beneficial. Particularly for games that have more than one Player sprite, it’s useful to make an event happen based on the sprite kind, rather than just the sprite name.
steps.instructions:
Code the tilemap border using a tilemap event.


Open Scenes and drag out an [on sprite overlaps tile] container. Keep the sprite kind set to “Player”, then set the tile to the one selected as the border in Step 1. Drag a [camera shake] block into the container and adjust the 2 parameters to control how much the screen will shake.


Right-click on the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of random tile] block from the [on start] container, select “Duplicate”, then drag the duplicated block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container. Replace (playerSprite) by dragging a (sprite) bubble into the parameter of the [place sprite on top of random tile] block.


Click ▶ then notice what happens when the Player sprite overlaps with the tilemap border!

steps.hints: ❓Did you drag the (sprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block so that every Coin sprite is placed on a random tile when it is created?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What happens if you do not drag the (sprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block? Does the block work?

❓How is using the [on created] container different than setting a sprite’s position in the [on start] container?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Using the lifecycle container can help categorize events and make clearer what should happen after certain actions. This is an example of organizing code into logical chunks, instead of putting all the code blocks in the [on start] container. Organizing code into meaningful events makes it easier for coders to debug or add to their existing code.

💡By using the [on created] container, the Ninja can reuse a chunk of code multiple times. In the next step, the Ninja will add code to respawn the Coin sprite when it is destroyed on overlap with the Player sprite. Now, the Coin sprite will be placed on a random tile, each time it is spawned.
steps.instructions:
Code the Coin sprite’s lifecycle to make it appear on a random tile when it is created.


Open Sprites, drag out an [on created] container, then change the sprite kind to Coin. 


Drag the Coin sprite’s [place sprite on top of random tile] block out of the [on start] container and into the [on created] container to make the Coin sprite start on a different tile every time it is created. Replace (coinSprite) by dragging a (sprite) bubble into the parameter of the [place sprite on top of random tile] block.


Click ▶ to see the Coin sprite appear on a random tile!

steps.hints: ❓Did you place the new [set sprite to] block under the [sprite start effect] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Coin sprite?

❓What happens if you do not drag the (sprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block? Does the block work?

❓How is using the [on destroyed] container different than using a [destroy sprite] block in an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Previously, the ninja may have used a [destroy sprite] block (with an effect) within an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. While similar in actions, using an [on destroyed] container can detach any subsequent effects from the destroy event itself and organize it separately.

💡When the Player sprite overlaps the Coin sprite, the Coin sprite will be destroyed with an effect, and then will respawn. The [on destroyed] container triggers the [set sprite to] block to run automatically upon each overlap.
steps.instructions:
When the Player sprite overlaps the Coin sprite, it doesn’t respawn! Continue coding the Coin sprite’s lifecycle to make something happen when it is destroyed.


Open Sprites and drag an [on destroyed] container, then change the sprite kind parameter to Coin. Drag a [sprite start effect] into the container, then update the effect and time parameter. Replace (mySprite) by dragging a (sprite) bubble into the parameter of the [sprite start effect] block.

 

Right-click on the Coin sprite’s [set sprite to] block from the [on start] container, select “Duplicate”, then drag the duplicated block into the [on destroyed] container to create a new sprite after the previous sprite was destroyed. 


The [destroy sprite] block in the [on (Player) overlaps (Coin)] container, from the starter code, will prompt the code inside the [on destroyed] container to run when the Player and Coin sprite overlap! 


Click ▶ to test out the game and watch what happens when the Coin sprite is destroyed!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Coin sprite’s lifespan in the  [on created] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens at the end of the Coin sprite’s lifespan?

❓ Why do you think the [set sprite lifespan] block might be useful to use in a game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The parameter in the [set sprite lifespan] block can be updated to make the sprite appear on the screen for shorter or longer intervals. Using milliseconds, the ninja can increase the value to make the lifespan longer, or decrease the value to make the lifespan shorter.
steps.instructions:
Code the Coin sprite’s lifespan to make it disappear, then reappear in a different position, if the Player does not reach it in time.


Drag a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on created] container, click ▼ in the blue rectangle to open the drop down menu and select [lifespan].  Replace (mySprite) by dragging (sprite) into the parameter of the [set sprite lifespan] block. Update the parameter to 2000, which refers to 2000ms or 2 seconds.


Click ▶ to test the game and watch the Coin sprite disappear if the Player sprite does not reach it in time! Try using different lifespan parameters, too!

steps.hints: ❓Did you put the [say] block inside the [forever] loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Did you select “lifespan” from the dropdown in the [set sprite x] block?

❓ Why might this be a useful feature to use in this game?

❓How is the [forever] loop different than the [on game update every ms] loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Similar to displaying other variables (such as score, lives, or countdown), it can be helpful to tell the user the value of a sprite’s lifespan as they are playing the game. Encourage the ninja to think about what else might be useful information for the user to know, as they are playing.
steps.instructions:
Watch the Coin sprite’s lifespan countdown on screen!


Open Loops then drag a [forever] loop container. Drag a [say] block inside the container and select the Coin sprite’s name.


Open Sprites and, drag a (sprite x) value block into the [say] block’s parameter. Change the sprite name to (coinSprite), then open the drop down menu to select [lifespan]. 


Click ▶ to see the Coin sprite’s lifespan countdown on screen! Grab the coin before the lifespan reaches 0!

subgroups.title: Coin Grabber!

namespace SpriteKind {
    export const Coin = SpriteKind.create()
}
sprites.onOverlap(SpriteKind.Player, SpriteKind.Coin, function (sprite, otherSprite) {
    otherSprite.destroy()
    music.play(music.melodyPlayable(music.baDing), music.PlaybackMode.UntilDone)
    info.changeScoreBy(1)
})

tiles.setCurrentTilemap(tilemap`level2`)
info.setScore(0)

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses tilemap and lifecycle events to code a collectible sprite that disappears if the Player does not reach it in time!

validationItems.text: Set the Player sprite to start on a random tile of one tilemap color, and the Coin sprite to start on a random tile of the other tilemap color.
Code the left and right direction buttons to move the Player sprite one tile left or right and change the image so the sprite is facing the correct direction.
Code the up and down direction buttons to move the Player sprite one tile up or down and change the image so the sprite is facing the correct direction.
Use an overlap event to code the tilemap border to shake the camera and move the Player sprite to a random tile.
Use an on created lifecycle event to create new Coin sprites and position them on a random tile after the previous sprite is destroyed.
Use an on destroyed lifecycle event to destroy the Coin sprite with an effect, then create a new Coin sprite.
Code the Coin sprite’s lifespan to start when it is created.
Have the Coin sprite “say” its countdown value as it updates.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about how to add events into your tilemap project. Events occur when a certain action triggers a set of code to run. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Party Planner
badges.description: Use events to control actions in a project with a tilemap.

badges.title: Trip Wire
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite overlaps a specific tilemap tile.

badges.title: Watch Out for That...!
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite hits a tilemap wall.

badges.title: New Tile Who Dis?
badges.description: Use an event to change a tile on a tilemap.

badges.title: Birthday Party
badges.description: Use an event to make something happen when a sprite is created.

badges.title: Farewell Party
badges.description: Use an event to make something happen when a sprite is destroyed.

badges.title: Ticking Clock
badges.description: Set a sprite’s lifespan in a project.
